hints: Think about what any electrode potential must be measured against, since a single half-cell voltage cannot be measured in isolation.
Recall the three standard condition values for concentration, gas pressure and temperature that make the potential a standard value.
walkthrough:
See why a reference is needed**
You can never dip a voltmeter into one beaker and read an absolute potential. A voltage is always a difference between two electrodes. By international agreement we give every half-cell a value relative to the hydrogen half-cell assigned $0.00 \text{ V}$.

Add the meaning of standard**
For the number to be $E^{\ominus}$ and not just $E$, all species must be in their standard states. That means dissolved ions at $1 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$, any gases at $1 \text{ atm}$ ($101 \text{ kPa}$) and a temperature of $298 \text{ K}$. Together this gives the definition: voltage of the electrode versus the standard hydrogen electrode under standard conditions.

Final answer: The voltage / e.m.f. of a half-cell compared to / connected to a standard hydrogen electrode.
Measured under standard conditions of $1 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ ion concentration, $1 \text{ atm}$ / $101 \text{ kPa}$ gas pressure and $298 \text{ K}$ / $25^{\circ}\text{C}$.

hints: Remember the positive terminal is connected to the half-cell with the more positive $E$ value, so use the + and - labels on each voltmeter to compare C with B and A with C.
walkthrough:
Read the + and - labels like a ranking**
In the left cell the $[\text{Ru(en)}_3]^{3+}/[\text{Ru(en)}_3]^{2+}$ electrode (C) is marked +, and the $[\text{Ru(NH}_3)_6]^{3+}/[\text{Ru(NH}_3)_6]^{2+}$ electrode (B) is marked -. So $E^{\ominus}(C) > E^{\ominus}(B)$. In the right cell the $[\text{Ru(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{3+}/[\text{Ru(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}$ electrode (A) is + and C is -. So $E^{\ominus}(A) > E^{\ominus}(C)$. Combining gives $B < C < A$, with B most negative and A least negative.

Final answer: most negative B, then C, then A least negative.
Order: B (most negative) above C above A (least negative).

hints: Picture an octahedral Ru centre with three bidentate en ligands, each en must span two adjacent positions to form a five membered chelate ring.
Think of the three chelate rings as blades of a propeller that can twist clockwise or anticlockwise to give non-superimposable mirror images.
Recall the name for stereoisomerism where two structures are mirror images that cannot be superimposed.
walkthrough:
Build the octahedral picture**
$\text{en}$, $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$, is bidentate, so each ligand donates two N lone pairs to Ru and bites at about $90^{\circ}$. Three en ligands therefore fill all six octahedral positions with three chelate rings. Draw Ru in the centre with one vertical bond up and down, then add the three N-N bridges around it in 3D using wedges and hashed bonds.

Create the pair of propellers**
If you look down the threefold axis the three rings look like a propeller. In isomer 1 the blades twist one way, in isomer 2 they twist the opposite way. The two drawings must be mirror images. No rotation can superimpose them, just like left and right hands. That is exactly what the mark scheme diagrams show.

Name the relationship**
Because the only difference is the non-superimposable mirror image arrangement around the same $\text{Ru(en)}_3$ connectivity, there is no cis trans or fac mer isomerism here. This is optical isomerism, and the two structures are a pair of enantiomers / optical isomers.

Final answer: Two 3D octahedral structures each with Ru at centre and three N-N chelate arcs occupying cis positions, drawn as non-superimposable mirror images (delta and lambda propeller forms).
Type of stereoisomerism: optical isomerism / enantiomerism.

hints: From the Data Booklet pick out $E^{\ominus}(\text{Br}_2/\text{Br}^-)$ and $E^{\ominus}(\text{Ag}^+/\text{Ag})$ and remember $E^{\ominus}_{cell} = E^{\ominus}_{positive} - E^{\ominus}_{negative}$ with electrons flowing from negative to positive.
walkthrough:
Calculate and assign polarity together**
From the Data Booklet $E^{\ominus}(\text{Br}_2/\text{Br}^-) = +1.07 \text{ V}$ and $E^{\ominus}(\text{Ag}^+/\text{Ag}) = +0.80 \text{ V}$. The more positive half-cell, bromine, is the cathode where reduction happens. So $$E^{\ominus}_{cell} = E^{\ominus}_{cathode} - E^{\ominus}_{anode} = 1.07 - 0.80 = +0.27 \text{ V}$$ Electrons in the external wire always flow from the negative anode (Ag) toward the positive cathode ($\text{Br}_2$).

Final answer: $E^{\ominus}_{cell} = 1.07 - 0.80 = +0.27 \text{ V}$
Direction of electron flow from $\text{Ag}^+/\text{Ag}$ half-cell to $\text{Br}_2/\text{Br}^-$ half-cell.

hints: Consider what adding water does to $[\text{Ag}^+]$ and therefore to the position of the $\text{Ag}^+(\text{aq}) + \text{e}^- \rightleftharpoons \text{Ag(s)}$ equilibrium.
Link a less positive $E(\text{Ag}^+/\text{Ag})$ to $E_{cell} = E_{cathode} - E_{anode}$ where Ag is the anode, to decide if $E_{cell}$ gets less positive or more positive.
walkthrough:
Follow the dilution**
Adding water lowers $[\text{Ag}^+]$. For $$\text{Ag}^+(\text{aq}) + \text{e}^- \rightleftharpoons \text{Ag(s)}$$ Le Chatelier tells you the system opposes the loss of $\text{Ag}^+$ by shifting left, making reduction less favourable. The electrode potential of the silver half-cell therefore becomes less positive.

Feed this into the cell e.m.f.**
Here Ag is the negative anode and $\text{Br}_2$ is the unchanged cathode. Since $$E_{cell} = E_{cathode} - E_{anode}$$ subtracting a smaller (less positive) $E_{anode}$ gives a larger difference. So $E_{cell}$ becomes more positive. Tick the more positive box.

Final answer: Tick: more positive.
$[\text{Ag}^+]$ decreases so $\text{Ag}^+/\text{Ag}$ equilibrium shifts to the left / $E$ for $\text{Ag}^+/\text{Ag}$ becomes less positive, so $E_{cell}$ increases.

hints: Focus on the electron pair behaviour that attaches a ligand to a central metal ion, not just on charge or size.
walkthrough:
Picture the bond forming**
A metal ion like $\text{Ag}^+$ has empty orbitals and acts as an electron pair acceptor. A ligand such as $\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}$ or $\text{NH}_3$ has a lone pair it can share. When that lone pair is donated into the metal to make a coordinate bond, the donor species is acting as a ligand.
Final answer: A species that donates / shares a lone pair of electrons to form a coordinate / dative covalent bond to a metal atom / ion.

hints: Write products over reactants with powers equal to stoichiometric numbers, remembering that pure solid AgBr does not appear in $K_c$.
walkthrough:
Apply the Kc rules to equilibrium 1**
For $$\text{AgBr(s)} + 2\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}(\text{aq}) \rightleftharpoons [\text{Ag(S}_2\text{O}_3)_2]^{3-}(\text{aq}) + \text{Br}^-(\text{aq})$$ put aqueous concentrations of products on top and reactants below. The solid $\text{AgBr}$ has constant concentration so it is omitted. The $2$ in front of $\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}$ becomes a square: $$K_c = \frac{[\text{Ag(S}_2\text{O}_3)_2^{3-}][\text{Br}^-]}{[\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}]^2}$$

hints: Recognise equilibrium 1 as the sum of AgBr dissolution ($K_{sp}$) plus complex formation ($K_{stab}$), so $K_c$ is the product of the two constants.
Multiply the numbers and check units by cancelling $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ terms from the $K_c$ expression to see what remains.
walkthrough:
Combine the constants**
Dissolution $\text{AgBr(s)} \rightleftharpoons \text{Ag}^+ + \text{Br}^-$ has $K_{sp}$, and $\text{Ag}^+ + 2\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-} \rightleftharpoons [\text{Ag(S}_2\text{O}_3)_2]^{3-}$ has $K_{stab}$. Adding the equations gives equilibrium 1, so multiply the constants: $$K_c = K_{sp} \times K_{stab} = (5.4 \times 10^{-13}) \times (2.9 \times 10^{13}) = 15.66 \approx 15.7$$

Sort out the units**
From (c)(ii), units are $\frac{(\text{mol dm}^{-3})(\text{mol dm}^{-3})}{(\text{mol dm}^{-3})^2}$ which all cancel. $K_c$ therefore has no units.

Final answer: $K_c = K_{stab} \times K_{sp} = (2.9 \times 10^{13}) \times (5.4 \times 10^{-13}) = 15.7$
units: none / no units / 1

hints: Compare the three $K_{stab}$ values: $5.3 \times 10^{18}$ for $[\text{Ag(CN)}_2]^-$, $2.9 \times 10^{13}$ for $[\text{Ag(S}_2\text{O}_3)_2]^{3-}$ and $1.6 \times 10^{7}$ for $[\text{Ag(NH}_3)_2]^+$.
Recall that a larger $K_{stab}$ means the complex formation equilibrium lies further to the right, so that complex will dominate when ligands compete for the same $\text{Ag}^+$.
walkthrough:
Rank by Kstab**
All three ligands compete for limited $\text{Ag}^+$. The $K_{stab}$ values differ by many powers of ten: $10^{18}$ versus $10^{13}$ versus $10^{7}$. The cyanide complex is overwhelmingly the most favoured, thiosulfate is next, and ammine is least favoured. So at equilibrium: $[\text{Ag(CN)}_2]^-$ highest, then $[\text{Ag(S}_2\text{O}_3)_2]^{3-}$, then $[\text{Ag(NH}_3)_2]^+$ lowest.

State the principle**
A larger stability constant means a more stable complex and a larger equilibrium concentration under identical ligand concentrations. That is why the order of concentrations follows exactly the order of $K_{stab}$ values.

Final answer: highest $[\text{Ag(CN)}_2]^-$ > $[\text{Ag(S}_2\text{O}_3)_2]^{3-}$ > $[\text{Ag(NH}_3)_2]^+$ lowest.
$K_{stab}$ for $[\text{Ag(CN)}_2]^-$ is highest so it is the most stable / higher $K_{stab}$ gives higher concentration of complex.
